title: Microbial Testing
subtitle: Counting microbes, and testing what kills them
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: design and conduct a practical investigation relating to the microbial testing of water or food samples
Conduct a laboratory experiment to assess the effect of antimicrobial treatment on the growth of microorganisms found in food or water
Conduct a scientific investigation to determine the effect of temperature on the viability of a non pathogenic E. coli
lessonIntent: Students can outline the serial dilution and plate count method, calculate CFU per mL, and design a valid, reliable experiment to test the effect of an antimicrobial treatment or of temperature on microbial growth.
examSkill: Calculate CFU per mL and percentage reduction from plate counts, and identify the variables, controls and safety steps in an antimicrobial or temperature investigation.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, microbial testing and antimicrobial treatments. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: Deadly water looks exactly like safe water
scenes.body: Water full of E. coli looks, smells, and tastes identical to clean water. The only way to know is to test.
scenes.callout: How do you detect an enemy you cannot see?
scenes.caption: Contaminated water is indistinguishable from safe water, so microbial testing is essential.

voiceover.text: Here's a sobering fact. Water carrying dangerous levels of E. coli, Salmonella or Cryptosporidium looks, smells and tastes exactly like perfectly safe water. The World Health Organization estimates contaminated drinking water causes around half a million diarrhoeal deaths every year. You can't see microbial contamination, and you certainly can't guess your way to safety. The only way to know is to test for the organisms directly, and then to test whether a treatment like chlorine or heat actually kills them. So how do scientists count an enemy they can't see? That's what we're building today.

scenes.heading: Why test, and why E. coli
scenes.body: Testing measures whether a sample carries harmful microbes, and at what concentration. E. coli is the key signal.

bullets.text: Safe drinking water: no E. coli detected in a 100 mL sample.
E. coli signals faecal contamination, so other pathogens may be present too.
It is chosen because it is easy to culture and easy to count.

scenes.secondary: E. coli is an indicator organism. It may not itself cause disease, but its presence reliably flags a sewage or animal-waste contamination event.
scenes.callout: One easy-to-count bug that warns of all the rest.
scenes.caption: Microbial testing measures harmful microbes; E. coli is the faecal indicator organism.

voiceover.text: So why test, and why is E. coli always the star? Microbial testing tells you whether a sample contains harmful microorganisms, and at what concentration. Australian drinking water guidelines say E. coli shouldn't be detected at all in a hundred millilitre sample. Here's the clever bit. E. coli lives in the gut, so finding it in water signals faecal contamination, which means more dangerous pathogens could be present too. That's why we call it an indicator organism, a warning flag for the whole group. And it's chosen for a practical reason as well, it's easy to culture and easy to count.

scenes.heading: The terms you need

bullets.text: Serial dilution: stepwise dilution of a sample to produce countable colonies.
Colony forming unit: a viable cell or cluster that grows into one visible colony.
Aseptic technique: methods that prevent contamination of samples and plates.
Antimicrobial treatment: anything that kills or inhibits microbes, e.g. chlorine, heat.
Viability: the ability of cells to survive and reproduce to form colonies.

scenes.callout: Dilute to count; one CFU is one visible colony.
scenes.caption: Serial dilution, colony forming unit, aseptic technique, antimicrobial treatment, viability.

voiceover.text: Five terms before the method. Serial dilution is diluting a sample again and again until the colonies become few enough to count. A colony forming unit, or CFU, is a viable cell, or a small cluster of cells, that grows into one visible colony on the agar. Aseptic technique is the set of methods that stop contamination, like sterile equipment and keeping plates closed. An antimicrobial treatment is anything that kills or slows the growth of microbes, such as chlorine, vinegar, an antiseptic or heat. And viability is whether cells can still survive and reproduce, which on a plate means whether they can still form a colony.

scenes.heading: Serial dilution and plate count
scenes.body: The core technique dilutes the sample until colonies are countable, then scales the count back up.

bullets.text: Collect a measured sample using aseptic technique.
Serially dilute: 1 mL into 9 mL gives a tenfold dilution each step.
Plate, incubate inverted, then count plates with 30 to 300 colonies.

scenes.secondary: Dilution is needed because a concentrated sample gives confluent, uncountable growth. Plates are inverted so condensation does not drip onto colonies.
scenes.callout: Too many to count? Dilute until you can.
scenes.caption: Collect, serially dilute tenfold, plate, incubate inverted, and count 30 to 300.

voiceover.text: Now the core technique, the serial dilution and plate count. First, you collect a measured volume of water, or a weighed food sample, using aseptic technique throughout. Second, you serially dilute. One millilitre of sample into nine millilitres of sterile water gives a one in ten dilution, and repeating that gives a hundredfold, then a thousandfold. Why bother? Because a heavily contaminated sample grows into one confluent, uncountable smear. Diluting spreads the colonies out, and the sweet spot is a plate with thirty to three hundred colonies. Third, you spread a measured amount onto nutrient agar, tape the lid, and incubate the plates upside down, so condensation doesn't drip onto your colonies. Finally, you count the plate that falls in that thirty to three hundred range.

scenes.heading: Calculate CFU per mL
scenes.question: A plate inoculated with 0.1 mL of a thousandfold (10 to the minus 3) dilution shows 156 colonies. Calculate the concentration of bacteria in the original sample, in CFU per mL.
scenes.coachNote: CFU per mL equals colony count divided by the volume plated times the dilution factor.
steps: Write the formula: CFU per mL = colony count ÷ (volume plated × dilution factor).
Express in standard form: 1.56 × 10 to the 6 CFU per mL.
Answer: the original sample held about 1.56 million bacteria per mL.
scenes.caption: 156 ÷ (0.1 × 10⁻³) = 1.56 × 10⁶ CFU per mL.

voiceover.text: Let's do the calculation the exam will ask for. A plate was inoculated with nought point one millilitres of a thousandfold dilution, that's ten to the minus three, and it shows one hundred and fifty six colonies. Find the concentration in the original sample. The formula is CFU per millilitre equals the colony count, divided by the volume plated times the dilution factor. Substituting, that's one hundred and fifty six divided by nought point one times ten to the minus three, which is one hundred and fifty six divided by nought point zero zero zero one. That gives one million, five hundred and sixty thousand CFU per millilitre, or one point five six times ten to the six in standard form. Notice how the units fall out, colonies over millilitres leaves CFU per millilitre.

scenes.heading: Testing an antimicrobial treatment
scenes.body: Plate counts become an experiment when you compare growth with and without a treatment.

bullets.text: Independent variable: the treatment, e.g. chlorine concentration or a vinegar wash.
Dependent variable: surviving CFU per mL, or zone of inhibition around a disc.
Controls: untreated sample for comparison; sterile water plate should grow nothing.
Keep constant: contact time, volume plated, agar, incubation temperature and time.

scenes.secondary: Run at least three replicates per treatment and average them. Keep plates sealed, incubate below body temperature, and autoclave or bleach used plates.
scenes.callout: Compare treated with untreated, and change only one thing.
scenes.caption: Antimicrobial experiment: treatment is the IV, surviving CFU per mL or inhibition zone is the DV, with untreated and sterile controls.

voiceover.text: Alright, counting is only half the story, because the new question is whether a treatment actually works. Say you want to know whether chlorine reduces the bacteria in creek water, or whether a vinegar wash reduces bacteria on lettuce. Your independent variable is the treatment, for example the chlorine concentration. Your dependent variable is the number of surviving bacteria, measured as CFU per millilitre after treatment. Another way to measure it is disc diffusion, where a paper disc soaked in the antimicrobial sits on a plate spread with bacteria, and you measure the clear zone of inhibition around it. Then the controls. An untreated sample gives you the baseline to compare against, and a sterile water plate should grow nothing, so any growth there means contamination. Keep the contact time, volume plated, agar, and incubation conditions the same, and run at least three replicates. For safety, keep plates taped shut, incubate below body temperature so you don't favour human pathogens, and autoclave or bleach used plates.

rows: Surviving CFU per mL, or inhibition zone

scenes.heading: Temperature and E. coli viability
scenes.body: Heat is an antimicrobial treatment too, and you can measure its effect with the same plate count.

bullets.text: Use a non-pathogenic school strain of E. coli, never an environmental sample.
Hold samples at a range of temperatures for a fixed time, then plate and count.
Viable counts stay high at moderate temperatures, then crash as heat denatures proteins.

scenes.caption: Heat-treat non-pathogenic E. coli at different temperatures, then plate and count survivors.

voiceover.text: So, heat works the same way, and there's a classic investigation for it. You take a broth culture of a non pathogenic E. coli strain, the kind supplied for school labs, and hold equal samples in water baths at a range of temperatures, say twenty, forty, sixty and eighty degrees, all for the same ten minutes. Then you dilute, plate and count, exactly as before. Here temperature is the independent variable and viable CFU per millilitre is the dependent variable. What you typically see is a count that stays high at moderate temperatures, then crashes once you get to around sixty degrees, because heat denatures the enzymes and other proteins the cells need to survive. That's the biology behind cooking food thoroughly and pasteurising milk.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: thinking one CFU always equals exactly one bacterial cell. A clump of cells can grow into a single colony.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: claiming a treatment works without an untreated control. Without a baseline, a low count proves nothing, because the sample may have been clean to begin with.
scenes.callout: One colony can be many cells; no baseline, no conclusion.
scenes.caption: One CFU may be several cells; an antimicrobial test needs an untreated control.

voiceover.text: Two traps to clear before we finish. Trap one, assuming one colony forming unit always equals exactly one bacterial cell. If several cells are clumped together when they land on the agar, they grow into a single colony, which is precisely why we say colony forming unit rather than cell. Trap two, claiming a treatment works without an untreated control. If your chlorinated sample shows few colonies, that proves nothing on its own, because the water might have been fairly clean to begin with. You need the untreated baseline, from the same sample, to show the treatment made the difference.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Untreated creek water: 0.1 mL of the 10⁻² dilution gives 180 colonies. After chlorination: 0.1 mL of the 10⁻¹ dilution gives 36 colonies. Calculate CFU per mL before and after, and the percentage reduction.
answerSteps: Both plates fall in the 30 to 300 range, so both counts are reliable.
Answer: chlorination reduced viable bacteria by 98% ✓
scenes.caption: 1.8 × 10⁵ to 3.6 × 10³ CFU per mL is a 98% reduction.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Untreated creek water, nought point one millilitres of the ten to the minus two dilution, gives one hundred and eighty colonies. After chlorination, nought point one millilitres of the ten to the minus one dilution gives thirty six colonies. Calculate the CFU per millilitre before and after, and the percentage reduction. Pause and work it through. Okay. Before, one hundred and eighty divided by nought point zero zero one is one point eight times ten to the five. After, thirty six divided by nought point zero one is three thousand six hundred. The reduction is the difference, divided by the starting count, times a hundred, which comes to ninety eight percent. And notice both plates sit in the thirty to three hundred range, so both counts are trustworthy. Chlorination cut the viable bacteria by ninety eight percent.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Microbial contamination is invisible; E. coli is the indicator of faecal contamination.
Serial dilution makes colonies countable; aim for 30 to 300 per plate.
CFU per mL = colony count ÷ (volume plated × dilution factor).
To test an antimicrobial, compare treated with untreated samples and change one variable.
Heat kills E. coli by denaturing proteins; viability crashes at high temperatures.
scenes.finalPrompt: Evaluating a microbial experiment? Check the variables, the controls, the replicates and the dilution maths.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: the indicator, dilution, the formula, antimicrobial design, temperature.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. First, microbial contamination is invisible, and E. coli is the indicator organism for faecal contamination. Second, serial dilution is what makes colonies countable, and you aim for a plate with thirty to three hundred. Third, CFU per millilitre equals the colony count divided by the volume plated times the dilution factor. Fourth, to test an antimicrobial treatment, you compare treated samples against an untreated baseline, changing only one variable and running replicates. And fifth, heat kills E. coli by denaturing its proteins, so viable counts crash at high temperatures. Whenever you evaluate a microbial experiment, check the variables, the controls, the replicates, and the dilution maths. See you next lesson.
